title: Probing the physical origins of 1/f noise by nonlinear transport
abstract: We report measurements of low frequency noise in the nonlinear electron transport of tunnel junctions that are dc or ac biased. We show that not only the resistance but also the nonlinear coefficients exhibit $1/f$-like noise, and that correlations among them exist. Using the common theoretical model for electron transport in tunnel junctions, we relate our measurements to fluctuations of barrier heights. We show in particular that the barrier heights on either side of the junction have strong fluctuations that are almost perfectly anti-correlated.
summary: This work investigates the source of $1/f$ noise in metal tunnel junctions by measuring noise across nonlinear transport coefficients. By applying the BDR model, the authors successfully link the observed noise spectra to fluctuations in the tunnel barrier heights. They conclude that the noise is dominated by strongly fluctuating, anti-correlated barrier heights, suggesting that new microscopic models are needed to explain this phenomenon.
main_problem: The paper aims to determine the physical origin of $1/f$ noise observed in the nonlinear electron transport characteristics of metal tunnel junctions.
main_result: The noise measurements confirm that both resistance and nonlinear coefficients exhibit $1/f$ noise, and the fluctuations are attributed to strongly fluctuating, almost perfectly anti-correlated barrier heights on either side of the junction.
method: The authors measured the low-frequency noise spectral density ($S_V(f)$) while biasing the junctions with both DC and AC currents, analyzing the resulting nonlinear coefficients ($R_0, R_1, R_2$).
model_or_system: The physical system is a metal tunnel junction (e.g., Al/AlOx/Al). The analysis is grounded in the Brinkman-Dynes-Rowell (BDR) model, which describes conductance based on barrier thickness ($d$), average height ($ ar{\varphi}$), and asymmetry ($\Delta\varphi$).
key_observables: Noise spectral density ($S_V(f)$), correlation between resistance fluctuations ($S_{i,j}^R(f)$), and the spectral densities of barrier height fluctuations ($S_{ ar{\varphi} ar{\varphi}}$, $S_{ ar{\varphi}\Delta\varphi}$, $S_{\Delta\varphi\Delta\varphi}$).
important_parameters: The noise exponent $\alpha$ (typically $1/f^{1.35}$), and the correlation coefficient $\sigma_{\varphi_1\varphi_2}$ between the barrier levels on either side.
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes that the barrier thickness ($d$) is constant while the barrier heights ($ ar{\varphi}, \Delta\varphi$) fluctuate, and that the correlation between $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ is frequency-independent.
figures_summary: Figures show the experimental setup, differential resistance vs. bias current, and raw/analyzed noise spectra under various DC and AC biases for both Al and Nb junctions.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by measuring noise across different bias conditions, relating the measured noise spectral densities of the nonlinear coefficients ($R_0, R_1, R_2$) back to the theoretical fluctuation spectra of the barrier parameters ($ ar{\varphi}, \Delta\varphi$), ultimately constraining the nature of the barrier height fluctuations.
why_interesting: While the primary focus is condensed matter noise physics, the detailed analysis of correlated fluctuations in barrier parameters provides a rigorous example of how microscopic disorder (barrier fluctuations) dictates macroscopic transport noise, which is relevant to understanding open quantum systems where environment coupling is key.
